summary:
LAST WORDS is an interactive, accessible digital storytelling platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Abandoned but not Forgotten). It chronicles the final transmissions, scientific breakthroughs, and enduring legacies of eight historic NASA machines resting on the Moon, Mars, and deep space—including Opportunity, InSight, Surveyor 3, and still-active beacons like Voyager 1 and Apollo 11’s laser retroreflector.

Addressing the challenge of discarded space hardware, LAST WORDS reframes so-called "space junk" into monuments of human curiosity and planetary archaeology. It features two distinct exploration modes: Little Explorers, offering illustrated storybooks, read-aloud narration, and STEM mini-games for young learners; and Mission Control, delivering primary telemetry logs, interactive "Then & Now" orbital imagery comparisons, and educator lesson plans. Every dramatized narrative is strictly verified against archival NASA flight data.

This project is vital because it bridges rigorous scientific data with emotional resonance, making space exploration accessible to all ages without logins, paywalls, or tracking. By honoring humanity’s robotic pioneers, LAST WORDS proves that being abandoned is never the same as being forgotten.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

LAST WORDS (https://last-words2.vercel.app/) is an interactive digital storytelling platform and virtual museum dedicated to eight historic NASA machines left on the Moon, Mars, and deep space (Surveyor 3, Apollo 17 ALSEP, Pioneer 10, Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, Apollo 11 Retroreflector, and Voyager 1).

The project operates through a dual-mode pedagogical engine:

  • 🚀 Little Explorers Mode (Ages 5–8 & Pre-readers): Presents picture-book story stages accompanied by an original animated companion named "Ping", browser-native Web Speech read-aloud narration, interactive WordBubbles for space vocabulary, tactile mini-games (Wipe the Dust, Fly Ingenuity, Catch the Signal, Moon Echo), and an instant-feedback sticker badge system.
  • 📡 Mission Control Mode (Grades 5–10, Educators & Enthusiasts): Features terminal-inspired "Final Logs" synchronized with dynamic radio carrier wave decay visualizers, verified "What Really Happened" telemetry timelines, interactive "Then & Now" orbital image comparison sliders (utilizing LROC and HiRISE imagery), and live Silence Clocks tracking elapsed time since final contact.
  • Technical Operation: Built as a zero-backend, statically compiled Next.js and TypeScript application deployed across a global edge network. All interactive calculations—such as the real-time 2.56-second lunar laser round-trip delay, Voyager 1's one light-day distance threshold (November 18, 2026), and telemetry audio synthesis—run entirely client-side using standard browser APIs without external server dependencies.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Scientific Integrity Over Sensationalism: It bridges literary storytelling and hard telemetry. Poetic media summaries (such as Opportunity's famous "My battery is low and it's getting dark") are juxtaposed with primary atmospheric optical depth (τ>10.8\tau > 10.8τ>10.8) and bus voltage logs, teaching students the difference between literary metaphor and engineering data.
  • Turnkey Educational Utility: Features a dedicated /teachers classroom module providing a 20-minute standards-aligned lesson plan (Hook, Explore, Debate, Exit Ticket), ethical debate prompts on planetary preservation vs. recycling, and print-optimized student worksheets and coloring sheets.
  • Universal Accessibility & Privacy: Compliant with WCAG 2.2 AA standards, featuring zero trackers, zero ads, zero external cookies, and complete offline capability via local browser storage.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Reframing Discarded Space Hardware: Transforms the public perception of lunar and Martian equipment from abandoned "cosmic junk" into revered monuments of human ingenuity and planetary archaeology.
  • Inspiring the Artemis & Mars Generation: Engages pre-readers and K-12 students alike by humanizing robotic explorers, sparking an early passion for aerospace engineering, planetary science, and software development.
  • Fostering Space Ethics & Heritage Literacy: Educates the public on critical, forward-looking space treaties and initiatives—such as the One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act, NASA's LunaRecycle Challenge, and repurposing rover hardware in the PROMISE lunar mission.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Framework & Languages: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript (Strict Mode), HTML5, CSS3.
  • Styling & Motion Physics: Tailwind CSS v4, custom keyframe animation physics, Lucide React icons.
  • Typography: Atkinson Hyperlegible (Braille Institute), Fredoka, Space Grotesk, and JetBrains Mono.
  • Web APIs & Audio: Web Speech API (speechSynthesis for read-aloud storytelling), native Web Audio API (custom dual-oscillator carrier wave synthesizer), and HTML5 Canvas (canvas-confetti).
  • Validation & Testing: Custom Node.js automated verification suite (scripts/validate-data.mjs), ESLint, and Puppeteer for cross-device visual audit (scripts/take-screenshots.mjs).
  • NASA Archives & Data: NASA Image & Video Library (images-api.nasa.gov), JPL Mission Telemetry Archives, NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS), NASA Science Directorate, ASU Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), and UArizona HiRISE.
  • Deployment & DevOps: Vercel Global Edge Network, Git, GitHub CLI, and Docker multi-stage containerization.

5. How is your project creative?

  • The "Dual-Audience" Adaptive Experience: Solves the challenge of wide age variance by offering an instant, one-click toggle between an inviting picture-book storybook for young children and a high-density, terminal-driven scientific telemetry dashboard for older students and adults.
  • Sensory Telemetry Storytelling: Instead of static paragraphs, final moments are experienced interactively: radio carrier waves flatline in real time as the user scrolls, and elapsed silence clocks underscore the profound isolation of deep space.
  • The "Still Answering" Hopeful Twist: Rather than ending on a somber note of abandonment, the project reveals that exploration never truly ceases: highlighting Voyager 1, which still transmits from interstellar space, and the Apollo 11 Retroreflector, which continues to bounce laser pulses back to Earth today with zero electrical power.
  • Experiential Mini-Games: Players do not just read facts—they physically simulate clearing Martian dust from Opportunity's solar panels, balance Ingenuity's altitude inside thin Martian air, and experience the speed-of-light delay to the Moon.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Universal Accessibility & Neurodiversity:
    • Integrated Calm Mode to eliminate all vestibular triggers, motion drifts, and sound effects for sensory-sensitive users.
    • Used the Atkinson Hyperlegible typeface to support low-vision readers, alongside a one-click typography scaler (A / A / A).
    • Designed child-friendly tap targets and implemented full screen-reader DOM support (sr-only narration buffers).
  • Strict Factual Guardrails: Every single machine entry is backed by an automated CI build test requiring at least two primary NASA/JPL/NTRS citations, verified UTC timestamps, and historical photographic credit.
  • Child Safety by Design: Eliminated all external third-party scripts, tracking pixels, logins, and remote databases. Children's sticker progress is saved purely in client-side localStorage.
  • Historical Nuance: Researched authentic archival documents, including declassified NTRS termination reports for the Apollo 17 ALSEP station and Pete Conrad's Apollo 12 inspection of Surveyor 3, illustrating that planetary equipment is protected heritage rather than discarded debris.
